# Core
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(kableExtra)
library(janitor)

# Specific models & utilities
library(caret)        # naive Bayes / random forest with tuned mtry
library(MASS)         # birthwt
library(rpart)        # CART
library(rpart.plot)   # tree plots
library(ranger)       # fast RF backend
library(glmnet)       # lasso / ridge
library(pdp)          # partial dependence
library(NHANES)       # Question 3
library(modeldata)    # ad_data, Question 4
library(torch)        # Question 4
library(luz)

# MASS masks dplyr::select; make sure select() means dplyr's
select <- dplyr::select

# Small helper: nice tables
kbl2 <- function(x, ...) kable(x, align = "lrrrrrr", ...) %>% kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

A helper to compute the metrics we’ve discussed (AUC is threshold-free; the others use a threshold, default 0.5). Note that I’ve added a warning if the AUC is less than \(0.5\).

eval_metrics <- function(truth, prob_pos, level_vals = NA, thr = 0.5) {
  if(is.na(level_vals)){
    if(!is.factor(truth)){
      if(identical(sort(unique(truth)), c(0,1))){
        level_vals <- c("0", "1")
      }else{
        stop("Truth must be a factor, binary 0/1, or the levels need to be given")
      }
    }else{
      level_vals = levels(truth)
    }
  }
  if(!is.factor(truth)){truth <- factor(truth, levels = level_vals)}
  cls   <- factor(ifelse(prob_pos <= thr, level_vals[1],level_vals[2]), levels = level_vals)
  res <- tibble(
    AUC  = roc_auc_vec(truth, prob_pos, event_level = "second"),
    Sens = sens_vec(truth, cls,        event_level = "second"),
    Spec = spec_vec(truth, cls,        event_level = "second"),
    PPV  = ppv_vec (truth, cls,        event_level = "second"),
    NPV  = npv_vec (truth, cls,        event_level = "second"),
    Acc  = accuracy_vec(truth, cls)
  )
  if(res$AUC < 0.5){warning(paste("The AUC is less than 0.5. Check the coding consistency. \n
                                  High probability currently means the subject is more likely", level_vals[1]))}
  return(res)
}

Question 1: Naive Bayes on dataset from UCI (Cleveland version)

Each row is a patient. Outcome Diagnosis is Benign or Malignant. Predictors are 30 numeric features derived from FNA images.

1(a) Explore the dataset

# --- Read the dataset from UCI (Cleveland version) ---
url <- "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/machine-learning-databases/heart-disease/processed.cleveland.data"

heart_raw <- read.csv(url, header = FALSE, na.strings = "?")

# --- Assign variable names based on UCI documentation ---
colnames(heart_raw) <- c(
  "age",        # age in years
  "sex",        # sex (1 = male; 0 = female)
  "cp",         # chest pain type (1–4)
  "trestbps",   # resting blood pressure (mm Hg)
  "chol",       # serum cholesterol (mg/dl)
  "fbs",        # fasting blood sugar > 120 mg/dl (1 = true; 0 = false)
  "restecg",    # resting electrocardiographic results (0–2)
  "thalach",    # max heart rate achieved
  "exang",      # exercise induced angina (1 = yes; 0 = no)
  "oldpeak",    # ST depression induced by exercise relative to rest
  "slope",      # slope of peak exercise ST segment (1–3)
  "ca",         # number of major vessels (0–3) colored by fluoroscopy
  "thal",       # 3 = normal; 6 = fixed defect; 7 = reversible defect
  "target"      # 0 = no disease; 1–4 = presence of heart disease
)


# --- Convert columns to appropriate types ---
heart_clean <- heart_raw %>%
  mutate(
    sex      = factor(sex, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Female", "Male")),
    cp       = factor(cp, levels = 1:4, labels = c("Typical", "Atypical", "Non-anginal", "Asymptomatic")),
    fbs      = factor(fbs, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("False", "True")),
    restecg  = factor(restecg, levels = 0:2, labels = c("Normal", "ST-T abnormality", "LVH")),
    exang    = factor(exang, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    slope    = factor(slope, levels = 1:3, labels = c("Upsloping", "Flat", "Downsloping")),
    ca       = as.numeric(ca),
    thal     = factor(thal, levels = c(3, 6, 7), labels = c("Normal", "Fixed", "Reversible")),
    target   = factor(ifelse(target == 0, "NoDisease", "Disease"))
  )

# --- Handle missing values ---
# Count missing (not much)
colSums(is.na(heart_clean))
     age      sex       cp trestbps     chol      fbs  restecg  thalach 
       0        0        0        0        0        0        0        0 
   exang  oldpeak    slope       ca     thal   target 
       0        0        0        4        2        0 
# Drop rows with missing values (most analyses do)
heart_final <- heart_clean %>% drop_na()

1(b) Train/Test Split

set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(heart_final, prop = 0.7)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

nrow(train); nrow(test)
[1] 207
[1] 90

1(c) Fit Naive Bayes (Caret)

train_control <- trainControl(
  method = "cv", 
  number = 10, 
  classProbs = TRUE,
  summaryFunction = twoClassSummary)

tune_grid <- expand.grid(
  laplace = c(0, 0.5, 1),
  usekernel = c(TRUE, FALSE),
  adjust = c(0.5, 1, 2)
)

set.seed(123)
fit_nb <- train(
  target ~ .,
  data = train,
  method = "naive_bayes",
  metric = "ROC",
  trControl = train_control,
  tuneGrid = tune_grid
)

fit_nb$bestTune
  laplace usekernel adjust
6       0      TRUE      2

1(d) Evaluate on Test Set

nb_pred_prob <- predict(fit_nb, newdata = test, type = "prob")[, "NoDisease"]
nb_pred_cls  <- predict(fit_nb, newdata = test)

nb_results <- eval_metrics(test$target, nb_pred_prob, thr = 0.5)
nb_results %>% kbl2(digits = 3)
AUC Sens Spec PPV NPV Acc
0.897 0.695 0.839 0.891 0.591 0.744

1(e) Re-fit with Binned Variables

# Example: bin Age and Cholesterol
heart_binned <- heart_final %>%
  mutate(
    AgeBin  = cut(age, breaks = c(0, 45, 55, 65, Inf), right = FALSE),
    CholBin = cut(chol, breaks = quantile(chol, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.25), na.rm = TRUE), include.lowest = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(-age, -chol)

split_h2 <- initial_split(heart_binned, prop = 0.7)
h2_tr <- training(split_h2)
h2_te <- testing(split_h2)

nb_fit2 <- caret::train(
  target ~ .,
  data = h2_tr,
  method = "naive_bayes",
  metric = "ROC",
  trControl = train_control,
  tuneGrid = tune_grid
)

nb2_prob <- predict(nb_fit2, newdata = h2_te, type = "prob")[, "NoDisease"]
nb2_cls  <- predict(nb_fit2, newdata = h2_te)

nb_results2 <- eval_metrics(h2_te$target, nb2_prob, thr = 0.5)

### Compare the results

nb_results %>% 
  mutate(Type = "Original", .before = AUC) %>% 
  bind_rows(
    nb_results2 %>% mutate(Type = "Binned", .before = AUC)
  ) %>% 
  kbl2(digits = 3)
Type AUC Sens Spec PPV NPV Acc
Original 0.897 0.695 0.839 0.891 0.591 0.744
Binned 0.925 0.727 0.891 0.865 0.774 0.811

Interpretation: Compare AUC/accuracy/sens/spec between raw vs. binned features; Naive Bayes can benefit when independence assumptions are closer to true after discretization.

1(f) When is Naive Bayes advantageous?

  • Works well with mixed data and small samples, robust with many predictors.

  • Fast baseline; often competitive when conditional independence is approximately satisfied.

  • In public health, good for quick triage models / risk screening where interpretability and speed matter.

2(c) Cross-Validation for cp

best_cp <- tree_fit$cptable[which.min(tree_fit$cptable[,"xerror"]), "CP"]
best_cp
[1] 0.04346711
tree_pruned <- prune(tree_fit, cp = best_cp)

2(d) Plot and Interpret Top Splits

rpart.plot(tree_pruned, extra = 101)

Interpretation (partial): The first split is on lwt, separating mothers with lwt < 110 vs lwt>= 110. In context, this suggests mother’s with lower weight in pounds at last menstrual period have babies that weigh less. The second split further differentiates for women who had lwt>= 110, for those that had presence of uterine irritability, their babies weighed less.

2(e) Compare RMSE to Linear Regression

set.seed(2)
split_bw <- initial_split(bw, prop = 0.8, strata = NULL)
bw_tr <- training(split_bw)
bw_te <- testing(split_bw)

# Fit/prune on training data using best_cp from full fit (simple approach)
tree_pruned_te <- predict(prune(rpart(bwt ~ ., data = bw_tr, method="anova",
                                      control = rpart.control(cp = best_cp)), cp = best_cp), newdata = bw_te)

lm_fit <- lm(bwt ~ ., data = bw_tr)
lm_pred <- predict(lm_fit, newdata = bw_te)

rmse_tree <- yardstick::rmse_vec(bw_te$bwt, tree_pruned_te)
rmse_lm   <- yardstick::rmse_vec(bw_te$bwt, lm_pred)
c(RMSE_tree = rmse_tree, RMSE_lm = rmse_lm)
RMSE_tree   RMSE_lm 
 719.3907  638.0250

2(f) Overfitting (Optional)

Deep trees can overfit noise (low training error, poor generalization). Using CP pruning via CV reduces leads to better generalization and lower test error.

Question 3: Random Forest and Penalized Regression — NHANES

We use the NHANES data from the dimension reduction example and predict body mass index (bmi), a continuous outcome.

3(a) Clean, Split, and Preprocess

We apply the cleaning code from the assignment. We then drop variables that would make the problem trivial or are redundant copies of other columns: weight and height (BMI is a deterministic function of the two), bmi_who (a categorized version of the outcome), id, age_decade (a binned age), hh_income (a categorized hh_income_mid), and the individual blood-pressure readings (bp_sys1-bp_dia3), which are summarized by bp_sys_ave and bp_dia_ave.

nhanes <- NHANES |>
  clean_names() |>
  distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(where(~ mean(is.na(.x)) <= 0.20)) |>
  drop_na() |>
  select(-id, -weight, -height, -bmi_who, -age_decade, -hh_income,
         -matches("^bp_(sys|dia)[123]$"))

dim(nhanes)
[1] 3727   18
names(nhanes)
 [1] "survey_yr"     "gender"        "age"           "race1"        
 [5] "hh_income_mid" "poverty"       "home_rooms"    "home_own"     
 [9] "bmi"           "pulse"         "bp_sys_ave"    "bp_dia_ave"   
[13] "direct_chol"   "tot_chol"      "urine_vol1"    "urine_flow1"  
[17] "diabetes"      "phys_active"  
set.seed(3)
split_nh <- initial_split(nhanes, prop = 0.7)
nh_tr <- training(split_nh)
nh_te <- testing(split_nh)

# no missing values remain, so the recipe only needs dummy coding and normalizing
rec_nh <- recipe(bmi ~ ., data = nh_tr) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

prep_nh <- prep(rec_nh)
nh_tr_baked <- bake(prep_nh, new_data = nh_tr)
nh_te_baked <- bake(prep_nh, new_data = nh_te)
c(train = nrow(nh_tr), test = nrow(nh_te), predictors = ncol(nh_tr_baked) - 1)
     train       test predictors 
      2608       1119         21

3(b) Fit a Random Forest (fixed ntree/mtry)

rf_spec <- rand_forest(mtry = 5, trees = 500, min_n = 5) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "permutation") |>
  set_mode("regression")

wf_rf <- workflow() |> add_model(rf_spec) |> add_recipe(rec_nh)
fit_rf <- fit(wf_rf, data = nh_tr)

3(c) Tune mtry via Cross-Validation

set.seed(3)
folds_nh <- vfold_cv(nh_tr, v = 5)
n_pred <- ncol(nh_tr_baked) - 1
grid_rf <- tibble(mtry = unique(round(seq(2, n_pred, length.out = 8))))

rf_tune_spec <- rand_forest(mtry = tune(), trees = 500, min_n = 5) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "permutation") |>
  set_mode("regression")

rf_tuned <- tune_grid(
  wf_rf |> update_model(rf_tune_spec),
  resamples = folds_nh,
  grid = grid_rf,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq)
)

collect_metrics(rf_tuned) |>
  filter(.metric == "rmse") |>
  select(mtry, mean, std_err) |>
  kbl2(digits = 3, caption = "5-fold CV RMSE by mtry")

3(d) Variable Importance

rf_obj <- extract_fit_parsnip(fit_rf_final)$fit

imp <- tibble(variable = names(rf_obj$variable.importance),
              importance = rf_obj$variable.importance) |>
  arrange(desc(importance))

imp |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  mutate(variable = fct_reorder(variable, importance)) |>
  ggplot(aes(importance, variable)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Permutation importance", y = NULL, title = "Top 10 predictors of BMI") +
  theme_minimal()

Interpretation: The top three predictors are age, direct_chol (HDL cholesterol), and bp_sys_ave (systolic blood pressure), with age and direct_chol close to tied and well ahead of the rest. Permutation importance measures how much the out-of-bag prediction error increases when a predictor is shuffled, so these are the variables whose information the forest relies on most. The importance does not give the direction of the association, and it can be shared among correlated predictors (blood pressure, cholesterol, and diabetes are all related to age and adiposity). Note that these are predictive associations, not causal effects.

3(e) Partial Dependence Plot

top_var <- imp$variable[1]
top_var
[1] "age"
pdp::partial(
  object          = rf_obj,
  pred.var        = top_var,
  train           = nh_tr_baked,
  grid.resolution = 30
) |>
  autoplot() +
  labs(y = "Predicted BMI", title = paste("Partial dependence:", top_var)) +
  theme_minimal()

Interpretation: Predicted BMI rises steeply from the youngest participants (about 12 years old) to around age 20, from roughly 26 to 29 kg/m\(^2\), and then levels off, increasing only slightly (about 29 to 30 kg/m\(^2\)) through the 70s. The partial dependence plot averages over the other predictors, so this is the average predicted BMI at each age, not an individual’s trajectory. The sharp rise followed by a plateau is a nonlinear shape a linear model would miss. Because the sample includes adolescents, a good part of the “age effect” reflects growth.

3(f) Penalized Regression

We fit a lasso with cv.glmnet() (5-fold CV on the training data) on the preprocessed predictors, and use the penalty that minimizes the cross-validated MSE (lambda.min).

x_tr <- as.matrix(select(nh_tr_baked, -bmi))
x_te <- as.matrix(select(nh_te_baked, -bmi))

set.seed(3)
cv_lasso <- cv.glmnet(x_tr, nh_tr_baked$bmi, alpha = 1, nfolds = 5)
cv_lasso

Call:  cv.glmnet(x = x_tr, y = nh_tr_baked$bmi, nfolds = 5, alpha = 1) 

Measure: Mean-Squared Error 

    Lambda Index Measure     SE Nonzero
min 0.0219    49   38.78 0.5860      20
1se 0.1696    27   39.30 0.4819      14
plot(cv_lasso)
plot(cv_lasso$glmnet.fit, xvar = "lambda", label = TRUE)
abline(v = log(cv_lasso$lambda.min), lty = 2)

The first plot shows the cross-validated MSE across the penalty path (the dotted lines mark lambda.min and lambda.1se), and the second shows the coefficient paths shrinking to zero as the penalty grows.

coef_lasso <- coef(cv_lasso, s = "lambda.min")
tibble(term = rownames(coef_lasso), estimate = as.numeric(coef_lasso)) |>
  filter(estimate != 0, term != "(Intercept)") |>
  arrange(desc(abs(estimate))) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  kbl2(digits = 3, caption = "Largest lasso coefficients (standardized predictors)")

3(g) Compare Test RMSE

rf_pred    <- predict(fit_rf_final, new_data = nh_te)$.pred
lasso_pred <- as.numeric(predict(cv_lasso, newx = x_te, s = "lambda.min"))

tibble(
  Model = c("Random forest", "Lasso"),
  Test_RMSE = c(rmse_vec(nh_te$bmi, rf_pred), rmse_vec(nh_te$bmi, lasso_pred)),
  Test_Rsq  = c(rsq_vec(nh_te$bmi, rf_pred),  rsq_vec(nh_te$bmi, lasso_pred))
) |> kbl2(digits = 3, caption = "Test-set performance")
Test-set performance
Model Test_RMSE Test_Rsq
Random forest 5.440 0.309
Lasso 5.607 0.256

Interpretation: The random forest has the lower test RMSE (about 5.4 vs. 5.6 kg/m\(^2\)) and higher \(R^2\) (0.31 vs. 0.26), so allowing for nonlinearity and interactions helps a little. Neither model predicts BMI very well, however: most of the variation in BMI is not explained by these variables. The lasso is nearly as accurate and is far easier to interpret (for instance, higher HDL cholesterol, male sex, and physical activity are associated with lower BMI, while age, diabetes, and blood pressure are associated with higher BMI). The cross-validated RMSE was also quite flat across mtry (6.16 to 6.23), so the choice of mtry matters little here.

Question 4: Neural Network — Alzheimer’s Disease (modeldata::ad_data)

4(a) Data, Split, Preprocessing, Tensors

data(ad_data, package = "modeldata")
ad <- ad_data |>
  as_tibble() |>
  # put the event ("Impaired") second so it is class 2 in torch and the "event" in yardstick
  mutate(Class = factor(Class, levels = c("Control", "Impaired")))

dim(ad)

There are 333 patients and 130 predictors (all numeric except the APOE Genotype), with no missing values. About 27% of patients are cognitively impaired, so the classes are moderately imbalanced. With so few patients and so many predictors, this is a hard setting for a neural network.

set.seed(4)
split1   <- initial_split(ad, prop = 0.6, strata = Class)
train_raw <- training(split1)
holdout   <- testing(split1)
split2   <- initial_split(holdout, prop = 0.5, strata = Class)
val_raw  <- training(split2)
test_raw <- testing(split2)

# preprocessing is learned on the training set only
rec <- recipe(Class ~ ., data = train_raw) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

prep_rec <- prep(rec)
train <- bake(prep_rec, train_raw)
val   <- bake(prep_rec, val_raw)
test  <- bake(prep_rec, test_raw)

c(train = nrow(train), validation = nrow(val), test = nrow(test), predictors = ncol(train) - 1)
     train validation       test predictors 
       199         66         68        134 
to_x <- function(d) torch_tensor(as.matrix(select(d, -Class)), dtype = torch_float())
to_y <- function(d) torch_tensor(as.integer(d$Class), dtype = torch_long())  # 1 = Control, 2 = Impaired

x_train_t <- to_x(train); y_train_t <- to_y(train)
x_val_t   <- to_x(val);   y_val_t   <- to_y(val)
x_test_t  <- to_x(test);  y_test_t  <- to_y(test)

# 0/1 outcomes for yardstick
y_train <- as.integer(train$Class) - 1
y_val   <- as.integer(val$Class)   - 1
y_test  <- as.integer(test$Class)  - 1

train_dl <- dataloader(tensor_dataset(x_train_t, y_train_t), batch_size = 32, shuffle = TRUE)
val_dl   <- dataloader(tensor_dataset(x_val_t,   y_val_t),   batch_size = 32, shuffle = FALSE)

n_features <- ncol(x_train_t)

4(b) A Flexible Network and a Fitting Function

make_mlp <- nn_module(
  initialize = function(n_in, hidden, p_drop) {
    layers <- list()
    prev <- n_in
    for (h in hidden) {
      layers <- c(layers, list(nn_linear(prev, h), nn_relu()))
      if (p_drop > 0) layers <- c(layers, list(nn_dropout(p = p_drop)))
      prev <- h
    }
    layers <- c(layers, list(nn_linear(prev, 2)))
    self$net <- do.call(nn_sequential, layers)
  },
  forward = function(x) self$net(x)
)

fit_mlp <- function(hidden, p_drop, wd, lr, max_epochs = 100, seed = 2026) {
  torch_manual_seed(seed)
  make_mlp |>
    setup(loss = nn_cross_entropy_loss(), optimizer = optim_adam) |>
    set_hparams(n_in = n_features, hidden = hidden, p_drop = p_drop) |>
    set_opt_hparams(lr = lr, weight_decay = wd) |>
    fit(train_dl, epochs = max_epochs, valid_data = val_dl, verbose = FALSE,
        callbacks = list(luz_callback_early_stopping(monitor = "valid_loss", patience = 8)),
        accelerator = accelerator(cpu = TRUE))
}

get_probs <- function(fitted, x_t) {
  fitted |>
    predict(x_t, accelerator = accelerator(cpu = TRUE)) |>
    nnf_softmax(dim = 2) |>
    as.matrix()
}

Training runs for up to 100 epochs but stops when the validation loss has not improved for 8 epochs. The number of epochs is therefore itself a (data-driven) form of regularization, alongside dropout and weight decay.

4(c) The Tuning Grid

We cross 5 architectures, 2 dropout rates, 3 weight-decay values, and 2 learning rates (60 networks). Models are ranked by validation AUC.

archs <- list(
  "4"        = 4,
  "8"       = 8,
  "8-4"    = c(8, 4),
  "16-8"    = c(16, 8),
  "16-8-4" = c(13, 16, 4)
)

grid <- expand_grid(
  arch   = names(archs),
  p_drop = c(0, 0.3),
  wd     = c(0, 1e-3, 1e-2),
  lr     = c(0.01, 0.001)
)

auc_of <- function(y, p) roc_auc_vec(factor(y, levels = c(0, 1)), p, event_level = "second")

# The grid is slow, so results are saved and reloaded on later renders.
# Delete hw4_tune_res.rds to re-run the search.
if (file.exists("hw4_tune_res.rds")) {
  tune_res <- readRDS("hw4_tune_res.rds")
} else {
  tune_res <- grid |>
    mutate(res = pmap(list(arch, p_drop, wd, lr), function(arch, p_drop, wd, lr) {
      f <- fit_mlp(archs[[arch]], p_drop, wd, lr)
      tibble(
        epochs    = length(f$records$metrics$valid),
        train_auc = auc_of(y_train, get_probs(f, x_train_t)[, 2]),
        val_auc   = auc_of(y_val,   get_probs(f, x_val_t)[, 2])
      )
    })) |>
    unnest(res) |>
    arrange(desc(val_auc))
  saveRDS(tune_res, "hw4_tune_res.rds")
}

dropout and/or weight decay 0.978 0.830 0.148 31.88
none 0.998 0.825 0.173 26.80

Reading the results.

  • Overfitting is everywhere. With 199 training patients and 134 predictors, nearly every network reaches a training AUC of about 1.0, while validation AUC is at most 0.88. Dropout and weight decay shrink the gap a bit (mean gap 0.148 vs. 0.173 with no regularization) and raise validation AUC slightly (0.830 vs. 0.825), but they do not cure it.
  • Many configurations are effectively tied. The validation set has only 66 patients (about 18 impaired), so the standard error of the validation AUC is several points. The top ten models are all within about 0.02 of each other, and there is no clear winner in architecture: a single hidden layer with 4 units, with dropout, does better than the two- or three-layer networks.
  • Winner’s curse: Because we picked the winner out of 60 candidates using the validation data, its validation AUC is optimistic.
best <- tune_res |> slice_head(n = 1)
best |> kbl2(digits = 3, caption = "Selected Configuration")
Selected Configuration

4 0.3 0.01 0.001 100 1 0.882

4(e) Lasso and Random Forest, and Thresholds

Both comparison models are tuned using the training data only (5-fold CV); the validation set is used, as for the network, to pick the classification threshold. The lasso logistic regression uses cv.glmnet() with cross-validated AUC as the criterion.

x_train <- as.matrix(select(train, -Class))
x_val   <- as.matrix(select(val,   -Class))
x_test  <- as.matrix(select(test,  -Class))

# Lasso logistic regression (the second level of Class, "Impaired", is the event)
set.seed(4)
cv_lasso <- cv.glmnet(x_train, train$Class, family = "binomial", alpha = 1,
                      type.measure = "auc", nfolds = 5)
cv_lasso

to_caret <- function(d) mutate(d, Class = factor(ifelse(Class == "Impaired", "yes", "no"),
                                                 levels = c("no", "yes")))
train_c <- to_caret(train); val_c <- to_caret(val); test_c <- to_caret(test)

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5, classProbs = TRUE,
                     summaryFunction = twoClassSummary)

# Random forest
set.seed(4)
rf_fit <- caret::train(
  Class ~ ., data = train_c, method = "rf", ntree = 500, metric = "ROC", trControl = ctrl,
  tuneGrid = data.frame(mtry = c(2, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, n_features))
)
rf_fit$bestTune

3   10
fit_best <- fit_mlp(archs[[best$arch]], best$p_drop, best$wd, best$lr)

p_val <- list(
  "Neural network" = get_probs(fit_best, x_val_t)[, 2],
  "Lasso"          = as.numeric(predict(cv_lasso, newx = x_val, s = "lambda.min", type = "response")),
  "Random forest"  = predict(rf_fit,    val_c, type = "prob")[, "yes"]
)

tune_threshold_j <- function(truth, prob) {
  truth <- factor(truth, levels = c(0, 1))
  js <- sapply(sort(unique(prob)), function(t) {
    cls <- factor(ifelse(prob >= t, 1, 0), levels = c(0, 1))
    as.numeric(sens_vec(truth, cls, event_level = "second") +
               spec_vec(truth, cls, event_level = "second") - 1)
  })
  sort(unique(prob))[which.max(js)]
}

thr <- sapply(p_val, function(p) tune_threshold_j(y_val, p))
thr

4(f) Test-Set Evaluation

The test set is used once, with the thresholds chosen on the validation set.

p_test <- list(
  "Neural network" = get_probs(fit_best, x_test_t)[, 2],
  "Lasso"          = as.numeric(predict(cv_lasso, newx = x_test, s = "lambda.min", type = "response")),
  "Random forest"  = predict(rf_fit,    test_c, type = "prob")[, "yes"]
)

map_dfr(names(p_test), function(m) {
  eval_metrics(y_test, p_test[[m]], thr = thr[[m]]) |>
    mutate(Model = m, Threshold = thr[[m]], .before = AUC)
}) |>
  select(Model, Threshold, AUC, Sens, Spec, Acc) |>
  kbl2(digits = 3, caption = "Final Test-Set Performance (thresholds from validation)")
Final Test-Set Performance (thresholds from validation)
Model Threshold AUC Sens Spec Acc
Neural network 0.450 0.743 0.632 0.796 0.750
Lasso 0.226 0.858 0.842 0.878 0.868
Random forest 0.406 0.889 0.421 0.980 0.824

Interpretation: On the test set, the random forest (AUC 0.89) and the lasso (AUC 0.86) are clearly better than the neural network (AUC 0.74), even though the network looked competitive on the validation set (0.88). That drop is the “winner’s curse” of choosing the best of 60 networks on 66 patients; the lasso (13 of 134 predictors kept at lambda.min) and random forest were tuned by cross-validation on the training data, so their numbers are less optimistic.

At the thresholds chosen on the validation set, the lasso gives the best balance of sensitivity (0.84) and specificity (0.88); the random forest has a slightly higher AUC but, at its threshold, a much lower sensitivity (0.42) with very high specificity (0.98). With only 19 impaired patients in the test set, each sensitivity rests on very few patients and has a wide confidence interval, and the AUC differences between the lasso and random forest are well within noise.

Recommendation: the lasso logistic regression, which performs about as well as the random forest, is simplest to explain, and selects a small, sparse set of biomarkers.

4(g) Discussion

  • Risks with this data. With only a few hundred patients and 130 predictors (more predictors than a reasonable number of events), a flexible network can fit the training data perfectly (as seen with a training AUC near 1), so performance estimates are noisy, tuning on a tiny validation set overfits the validation data, and results depend heavily on the random split and initialization. Thresholds chosen on so few patients are unstable. Cross-validation, repeated splits, or averaging over seeds would give more trustworthy comparisons.
  • When neural networks are overkill. When data are small or low-dimensional, tabular, and mostly smooth or linear in the predictors, penalized regression, trees, or random forests usually match a neural network and are far easier to tune, explain to clinicians, and validate, as we saw here. Networks tend to pay off with very large samples or unstructured inputs such as images (the chest X-ray example), text, or signals. In public health, interpretability, calibration, and the ability to audit a model for fairness often matter as much as a small gain in AUC.

Question 5: Global versus Local Structure

You are studying a dataset of 500 patients, each with 200 biomarkers measured at baseline. You plan to visualize the relationships between individuals using a low-dimensional embedding (2D or 3D). Consider the following situations and state whether a global or local dimension reduction method would be more appropriate. Justify your answer in 2–3 sentences.

  1. You believe there is a single underlying continuous “disease severity” score that explains most of the biomarker variation.

Because the goal is to uncover a single latent “disease severity” construct that drives the biomarker patterns across all patients, a global dimension reduction method is most appropriate. Global methods (e.g., PCA, factor analysis) capture the dominant sources of variation in the entire dataset and can reveal overarching continuous scores that summarize overall severity.

  1. You are interested in identifying small subgroups of patients with very similar biomarker profiles but distinct from the rest of the population.

Here the goal is to detect small, homogeneous subgroups of patients who differ from the rest of the population, so a local dimension reduction method is more suitable. Local methods (e.g., UMAP, t-SNE, Isomap) preserve neighborhood structure and emphasize local similarities, making them effective for revealing subtle clusters that global methods may smooth over.

  1. You plan to create a 2D visualization of single-cell RNA expression data to identify cell-type clusters.

For visualizing single-cell RNA-seq data and identifying cell-type clusters, a local dimension reduction method such as t-SNE or UMAP is appropriate. These methods preserve fine-grained local relationships and therefore allow biologically similar cells to cluster together in low-dimensional space, whereas global methods often miss these subtle but important boundaries.

  1. You have time-series physiological data (e.g., heart rate, sleep, and activity) and want to summarize the overall level and variability across participants.

If the goal is to summarize broad patterns–such as overall levels and variability in time-series physiological measures across participants–a global dimension reduction method is most appropriate. Global methods highlight major sources of variation shared across the dataset and provide low-dimensional summaries of overall behavior rather than focusing on small local deviations.
